scope: Eight original AS Physics 7408 3.2.1.2, 3.2.1.5 and 3.2.1.7 equations/conservation questions (not copied AQA papers)
notes: Where full nuclide notation or handwritten equations are assessed, manual review is explicitly required; other automatic rubric suggestions are provisional. Correct conservation totals are necessary but do not imply energy-momentum feasibility. Each mark point is individually checkable.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.series: Original AQA-style Nuclear Equations and Conservation
questions.question: Fully balanced radium alpha-decay equation
questions.prompt: A radium-226 nucleus (Z = 88) undergoes alpha decay, forming radon (Z = 86). Write the full balanced nuclear equation, using nucleon and proton numbers on each symbol. Show separately how the A and Z totals balance. [5 marks]
markPoints: The starting nuclide is written correctly as ²²⁶₈₈Ra.
The daughter nuclide is written as ²²²₈₆Rn.
The emitted alpha particle is correctly represented as ⁴₂He or ⁴₂α.
All three products and reactants appear on their correct sides of a nuclear decay arrow.
Balances A: 226=222+4 and Z: 88=86+2, both shown or explicitly demonstrated.
questions.modelAnswer: ²²⁶₈₈Ra → ²²²₈₆Rn + ⁴₂He. The total nucleon number is 226 on each side (222+4); total proton number 88 on each side (86+2).

questions.subject: Physics
questions.series: Original AQA-style Nuclear Equations and Conservation
questions.question: Balanced carbon-14 beta-minus equation
questions.prompt: Carbon-14 (Z = 6) undergoes beta-minus decay to a nitrogen nucleus (Z = 7). Write a complete balanced nuclear decay equation with all necessary emitted particles, then explain why an electron antineutrino is needed. [5 marks]
markPoints: Correct initial carbon nuclide ¹⁴₆C.
Correct nitrogen daughter nuclide ¹⁴₇N, with the SAME A=14.
Electron e⁻ (or β⁻) included as an emitted particle with charge −1.
Electron antineutrino ν̄ₑ included, not an electron neutrino νₑ.
Conservation of charge and electron-lepton number is explained: initial charge 6 and Lₑ=0; final charges 7−1=6 and lepton numbers +1−1=0.
questions.modelAnswer: ¹⁴₆C → ¹⁴₇N + ⁰₋₁e + ν̄ₑ. Nucleon number is 14 both sides. Charge balances because 6=7−1. The electron has electron-lepton number +1 and the electron antineutrino −1, so electron-lepton number remains zero. The (anti)neutrino is also needed to account for the continuous beta-energy spectrum.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.series: Original AQA-style Nuclear Equations and Conservation
questions.question: Check three conservation laws in free-neutron decay
questions.prompt: A free neutron undergoes n → p + e⁻ + ν̄ₑ. Explain, with numerical initial and final totals, how electric charge, baryon number and electron-lepton number are conserved. State the quark flavour change and why the antineutrino cannot be replaced by a neutrino. [6 marks]
markPoints: Electric charge initial 0 and final +1−1+0=0.
Baryon number initial +1 and final +1+0+0=+1.
Electron-lepton number initially 0; electron contributes +1 and antineutrino contributes −1, summing to 0.
A down quark changes into an up quark in the neutron (udd → uud).
Replacing ν̄ₑ by νₑ would give final electron-lepton number +2, which violates conservation.
Identifies weak decay, with W⁻ exchanged/emitted at quark conversion (or an equivalent correct account).
questions.modelAnswer: Charge: 0→(+1−1+0)=0. Baryon number: +1→(+1+0+0)=+1. Electron-lepton number: 0→(0+1−1)=0. In the weak interaction d→u+W⁻, and W⁻ produces e⁻+ν̄ₑ. A neutrino instead would carry Lₑ=+1, producing Lₑ=+2, so it is forbidden.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.series: Original AQA-style Nuclear Equations and Conservation
questions.question: Test beta-plus conservation in a proton-to-neutron transition
questions.prompt: Consider p → n + e⁺ + νₑ inside a suitable proton-rich nucleus. Use numerical particle charges, baryon numbers and electron-lepton numbers to prove that this is allowed by those three conservation laws. Explain why the proton-to-neutron quark conversion is u → d. [5 marks]
markPoints: Charge conserved: +1 initially and 0+1+0=+1 finally.
Baryon number conserved: +1 initially and +1+0+0=+1 finally.
Electron-lepton number conserved: 0 initially and −1+1=0 finally.
Correct quark change u → d, converting uud proton to udd neutron.
Notes that conservation of these quantum numbers alone does not make decay of an isolated free proton energetically possible: the nuclear energy balance matters.
questions.modelAnswer: Charge +1=0+1+0; baryon number +1=+1+0+0; electron-lepton number 0=0−1+1. u→d makes uud→udd through the weak interaction. Free proton beta-plus decay is not energetically permitted; the process can occur in a suitable nucleus if its energy balance allows it.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.series: Original AQA-style Nuclear Equations and Conservation
questions.question: Strong production of an oppositely strange pair
questions.prompt: In a sufficiently energetic collision, two pions undergo π⁺ + π⁻ → K⁺ + K⁻. Data: pion baryon number 0, strangeness 0; K⁺ has strangeness +1 and charge +1; K⁻ has strangeness −1 and charge −1. Check the initial and final charge, baryon number and total strangeness. Explain why this reaction is compatible with a strong interaction, without assuming the provided data alone guarantees sufficient collision energy. [5 marks]
markPoints: Initial electric charge +1−1=0 and final +1−1=0.
Both initial and final baryon numbers are 0.
Initial total strangeness is 0 and final strangeness +1−1=0.
Explains that strange particles are created as a pair with net strangeness zero in a strong interaction.
Correctly distinguishes conservation-law allowance from energy/momentum feasibility; sufficient collision energy is still needed.
questions.modelAnswer: Charge: 0→0. Baryon number: 0→0. Strangeness: 0→(+1−1)=0. Producing K⁺ and K⁻ together preserves strangeness, as required in the strong interaction. Kinematic feasibility also requires enough centre-of-mass energy and conservation of momentum.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.series: Original AQA-style Nuclear Equations and Conservation
questions.question: Weak decay of a strange meson
questions.prompt: Consider the decay K⁺ → π⁺ + π⁰. Data: K⁺ has Q=+1, baryon number 0, strangeness +1; both pions have baryon number and strangeness zero; π⁺ has charge +1 and π⁰ has charge zero. Check three conservation quantities and identify which fundamental interaction can mediate the decay. [5 marks]
markPoints: Initial total charge +1 equals final +1+0.
Initial baryon number 0 equals final 0+0.
Strangeness changes from +1 to 0, so ΔS=−1.
Explains that strong interactions conserve strangeness and hence cannot cause this change.
Identifies the weak interaction as permitting ΔS=±1 (or zero) while maintaining the other required conservation laws.
questions.modelAnswer: Charge +1→(+1+0)=+1; baryon number 0→0. Strangeness +1→0 so ΔS=−1. The decay is weak: a strong interaction would conserve strangeness. Total energy and momentum must also be conserved.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.series: Original AQA-style Nuclear Equations and Conservation
questions.question: Diagnose an impossible proposed particle reaction
questions.prompt: A student proposes e⁻ + π⁺ → p + γ. Data: e⁻ has Q=−1, B=0, electron-lepton number +1; π⁺ has Q=+1, B=0, Lₑ=0; p has Q=+1, B=+1, Lₑ=0; photon γ has Q=B=Lₑ=0. Use the information to identify every violated conserved quantity. Explain why adding more collision energy cannot make the proposed products correct. [5 marks]
markPoints: Initial charge −1+1=0, but final charge +1+0=+1; electric charge is violated.
Initial baryon number 0 but final baryon number +1; baryon number is violated.
Initial electron-lepton number +1, final total 0; electron-lepton number is violated.
States that a physically allowed interaction must conserve ALL applicable quantities simultaneously.
More energy does not remove these conservation requirements; the proposed products cannot be the complete final state.
questions.modelAnswer: Charge initial 0, final +1: not conserved. Baryon number initial 0, final +1: not conserved. Electron-lepton number initial +1, final 0: not conserved. No extra collision energy makes that final state possible because these conservation laws are exact within this model; additional final particles would be needed for a different reaction.

questions.subject: Physics
questions.series: Original AQA-style Nuclear Equations and Conservation
questions.question: Quark charges and weak beta conversion
questions.prompt: The up and down quarks have charges +2/3 e and −1/3 e respectively. Find the charges of uud and udd quark combinations. Explain which gives the proton and which the neutron. During beta-minus decay, identify the one quark that changes, the emitted weak boson and the charged lepton produced from it. [6 marks]
markPoints: Charge of uud is (2/3+2/3−1/3)e=+e.
Charge of udd is (2/3−1/3−1/3)e=0.
Correctly identifies uud as proton and udd as neutron.
In beta-minus decay one d quark becomes u, so neutron udd becomes proton uud.
A W⁻ boson is emitted at d → u, preserving charge at that vertex.
W⁻ leads to an outgoing electron e⁻ and electron antineutrino ν̄ₑ.
questions.modelAnswer: uud: +2/3+2/3−1/3=+1, so uud is the proton. udd: +2/3−1/3−1/3=0, so udd is the neutron. In beta-minus decay d→u+W⁻, and W⁻ produces e⁻ and ν̄ₑ. Total charge and electron-lepton number remain conserved.
